stances.claim: The CPRA's six canons collapse into three duty-groups: (1) independence and propriety; (2) fidelity; and (3) competence, diligence, equality, and accountability -- a usable structural map for lay readers.
stances.rhetorical_move: structural-map simplification of six canons into three duty-groups

stances.claim: Under independence (Canon I), lawyers must act with integrity on the merits and resist client procedural dictation -- though they must respect client decisions to settle or compromise after explaining consequences; under propriety (Canon II), they must avoid all unlawful/dishonest/immoral/deceitful conduct and all forms of abuse, and use dignified, gender-fair, child- and culturally-sensitive language.

The law profession is not a business -- PH uniquely prohibits ambulance-chasing and open hawking; permissible advertising must be dignified, verifiable, factual, and non-self-laudatory; no payments to media practitioners or award-giving bodies to attract legal representation.

Public prosecutors have a special duty under the CPRA: their primary duty 'is not to convict but to see that justice is done' -- a critical professional-identity formulation for prosecutorial restraint.
stances.rhetorical_move: verbatim canon-citation of a high-stakes-prosecutorial-duty principle

stances.claim: Under fidelity (Canon III), the lawyer-client relationship arises when the client consciously, voluntarily, and in good faith vests the lawyer with confidence -- this explains, in part, why CJ declines to render advice on specific cases referred by readers and always redirects them to a competent lawyer, the PAO, or the IBP.

Equality (Canon V) prohibits client decline on grounds of nationality, ethnicity, sexual orientation or gender identity, religion, disability, age, marital status, social or economic status, political beliefs, or even the lawyer's or public's opinion regarding the guilt of the person -- and prohibits refusing indigents except for narrowly justifiable reasons (capacity, conflict, or close-degree relation).

Accountability (Canon VI) operates via confidential, summary process at the SC and/or IBP, with the complainant bearing the burden of substantial evidence -- 'the amount of relevant evidence which a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to justify a conclusion' -- not proof beyond reasonable doubt.

notable_anecdotes: The CJ-declines-to-render-advice self-disclosure -- 'This duty explains, in part, why I decline to render advice or opinion on specific problems or cases referred to me by my esteemed readers. I always ask them to consult a competent lawyer, or the Public Attorney's Office (PAO), or the Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP).' -- using a CPRA canon to explain CJ's own column policy.

The PH-exceptionalist business-vs-profession framing -- 'Unlike other countries, the Philippines does not allow ambulance-chasers or the open selling/hawking of services' -- flagging the cultural-legal divergence from US-style legal marketing.
The public-prosecutor's principle -- 'is not to convict but to see that justice is done' -- a single-sentence canon quote that captures the prosecutorial-restraint ethic.

The lawyer-client romantic-relations prohibition -- 'shall not have dating, romantic, or sexual relations with a client during the engagement, unless the consensual relationship existed between them before the lawyer-client relationship commenced' -- surfaced as the most explicit personal-conduct CPRA rule.

The PAO marginalized-sector conflict-imputation rule -- that PAO conflicts impute only to the lawyer directly handling and the supervisor, not disqualifying the rest of PAO -- a structural design to keep marginalized parties from being unrepresented.

The substantial-evidence standard for disciplinary cases -- 'the amount of relevant evidence which a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to justify a conclusion' -- explicitly distinguished from criminal proof beyond reasonable doubt.

one_paragraph_summary: Continuing his CPRA series, Panganiban summarizes the duties of lawyers under the new 56-page Code, simplifying its six canons into three duty groups: (1) independence and propriety; (2) fidelity; and (3) competence, diligence, equality, and accountability. Under independence (Canon I), lawyers must act with integrity and rely solely on the merits, not allowing the client to dictate procedure while still respecting the client's decision to settle or compromise after explaining consequences. Under propriety (Canon II), lawyers shall not engage in unlawful, dishonest, immoral, or deceitful conduct, nor in physical, sexual, psychological, or economic abuse, and must use dignified, gender-fair, child- and culturally-sensitive language. The law profession is not a business -- PH, unlike other countries, does not allow 'ambulance-chasers' or open hawking; advertising must be dignified, verifiable, factual, and non-self-laudatory, with no payments to media practitioners or award-giving bodies. The primary duty of public prosecutors 'is not to convict but to see that justice is done.' Under fidelity (Canon III), the lawyer-client relationship arises when the client consciously, voluntarily, and in good faith vests the lawyer with confidence -- which explains, in part, why CJ declines to render advice on specific cases referred by readers and always redirects them to a competent lawyer, the PAO, or the IBP. Fidelity prohibits representing conflicting interests except with all concerned parties' written informed consent and prohibits dating/romantic/sexual relations with a client during engagement (unless preexisting). PAO's marginalized-sector access is protected by limiting conflict imputation to the lawyer directly handling and the supervisor only. Under Canon IV, lawyers must observe competence, diligence, commitment, and skill regardless of fee or pro bono status, with lifelong learning required even when engaged in another profession or business. Under Canon V on equality, a lawyer cannot decline a client based on nationality, ethnicity, sexual orientation or gender identity, religion, disability, age, marital or social or economic status, political beliefs, or even the lawyer's or public's opinion on the person's guilt, with narrowly defined exceptions (capacity, conflict, sixth-degree relation to adverse party, fourth-degree to adverse counsel). Canon VI provides for accountability via confidential, summary process at the SC and/or IBP, with the complainant bearing the burden of substantial evidence -- 'the amount of relevant evidence which a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to justify a conclusion' -- not proof beyond reasonable doubt.
